title: Sprouted Potatoes: When You Can Use Them and When to Throw Them Away

seo.title: Are Sprouted Potatoes Safe to Eat?
seo.meta_description: Small sprouts can sometimes be removed from a firm, non-green potato, but heavily sprouted, green, shriveled or bitter potatoes should be discarded.
seo.search_intent: Food safety decision about sprouted potatoes.

excerpt: A firm potato with only tiny sprouts and no green areas can often be used after the sprouts, eyes and surrounding peel are removed generously. Heavily sprouted, green, shriveled or bitter potatoes are better discarded because glycoalkaloids may be elevated.
content_html:
Sprouting is normal potato biology, but sprouts are not just cosmetic. Potato sprouts and nearby tissues can contain high levels of natural defense compounds called glycoalkaloids, especially alpha-solanine and alpha-chaconine.

When a lightly sprouted potato can be used

If the potato is still firm, has no green areas and only small sprouts, remove each sprout, the eye beneath it and a generous amount of surrounding peel. EFSA guidance advises removing sprouts and damaged or rotten areas.

When to discard it

  • Large green areas.
  • Many long sprouts.
  • Severe shriveling or softness.
  • Extensive rot.
  • Strong bitter taste or burning sensation.

Why glycoalkaloids matter

High exposure can cause acute gastrointestinal symptoms including nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. EFSA identified 1 mg/kg body weight per day as the lowest observed adverse effect level in its assessment.

Can cooking make a heavily sprouted potato safe?

Do not rely on it. EFSA reports wide reductions from peeling, boiling and frying, but processing does not provide a simple guarantee. A very green or heavily sprouted potato is not worth rescuing.

Store potatoes in the dark

Light encourages greening and can coincide with rising glycoalkaloids. A cool, dark, dry and ventilated storage area slows both sprouting and quality loss.

A simple decision guide

Potato conditionPractical choice
Firm, no green areas, one or two tiny sproutsRemove sprouts, eyes and surrounding peel generously; use promptly
Many long sproutsDiscard
Green skin or green fleshDiscard
Very soft, shriveled or rottenDiscard
Noticeably bitter or causes oral burningDo not continue eating; discard

The table is intentionally conservative. A home cook cannot measure glycoalkaloid concentration by looking at a potato, so appearance, texture and storage history are used as practical signals.

Sprouts are more than a quality issue

As a potato breaks dormancy, it uses stored carbohydrate to grow shoots. The sprouts themselves and the tissue around the eyes can contain much higher concentrations of glycoalkaloids than the inner flesh. That is why simply snapping off the visible tip is not enough; the eye and surrounding peel should also be removed when the rest of the potato is still firm and non-green.

A heavily sprouted potato is a different situation. Once there are many long shoots, substantial shriveling or green tissue, there is little reason to try to rescue it. The food-quality loss and uncertainty about glycoalkaloids outweigh the value of saving one potato.

How much can peeling and cooking reduce glycoalkaloids?

EFSA reports wide ranges rather than one fixed number. Peeling can reduce glycoalkaloids by about 25–75%, boiling by roughly 5–65%, and frying in oil by around 20–90%. Those ranges are broad because the starting concentration, potato variety and processing conditions differ.

This is why cooking should not be treated as a rescue guarantee. A 25% reduction is very different from a 75% reduction, and neither tells you the starting concentration in a particular heavily sprouted potato.

What does the 1 mg/kg adverse-effect level mean?

EFSA identified 1 mg of glycoalkaloids per kilogram of body weight per day as the lowest observed adverse effect level in its assessment. For a 70 kg adult, that corresponds mathematically to 70 mg. It is not a household “safe allowance,” because you do not know how many milligrams are present in a suspicious potato and sensitivity varies.

The number is useful for understanding why children can be more vulnerable: the same amount of glycoalkaloids represents a larger dose per kilogram of body weight in a smaller person.

How to slow sprouting at home

Keep potatoes in a dark, dry and ventilated place and avoid prolonged light exposure. Buy quantities you can realistically use before they become soft and heavily sprouted. Check the bag periodically and remove rotten potatoes so they do not accelerate deterioration of the rest.

Bottom line

A tiny sprout on an otherwise firm, non-green potato is not the same as a potato covered in long shoots. The first can often be used after generous trimming; the second should be discarded. Greening, severe shriveling, rot and bitterness all push the decision toward throwing the potato away rather than relying on cooking to fix it.

Frequently asked questions

Can I eat a potato with one small sprout?

Usually if it remains firm and non-green after the sprout, eye and surrounding peel are removed generously.

Are the sprouts edible?

No. Remove them; they can contain high glycoalkaloid concentrations.

Does boiling remove solanine?

It can reduce glycoalkaloids to a variable degree, but it should not be used to justify eating a heavily green or sprouted potato.

faq.question: Can you eat a potato with a small sprout?
faq.answer: A firm, non-green potato with a tiny sprout can often be used after removing the sprout, eye and surrounding peel generously.

faq.question: When should a sprouted potato be discarded?
faq.answer: Discard heavily sprouted, green, very soft/shriveled, rotten or bitter potatoes.

faq.question: Does cooking remove glycoalkaloids?
faq.answer: Cooking and peeling can reduce them variably, but do not make heavily green or sprouted potatoes a good choice.
